cultivar: Shui Xian (bushes typically 50–60 years old or more)
processing: Standard Wuyi yancha processing from unusually large, thick leaves: medium oxidation, strip rolling and a medium to heavy charcoal roast, often in two or three passes with rests in between.
harvest_season: One spring picking, usually in early to mid-May; old bushes sprout later and yield less than young plantings.
appearance_dry: Very long, broad, loosely twisted dark strips, sometimes with thick stems, and a dry, woody-sweet smell.
appearance_liquor: Deep amber to reddish-orange, clear, with a visible thickness when poured.
appearance_wet: Big leathery leaves, olive to dark brown with red edges, thick-veined and slow to open.
taste_profile: Deeply smooth with a woody, mossy old-bush note (cong wei), dark honey and orchid, and a cooling, resinous finish that goes on for minutes.

brewing.notes: Boiling water and a zisha pot if you have one; the thick leaf likes heat. Rinse briefly, then keep early steeps short. The old-bush character shows most in the aftertaste and in the cooled cup, so sip slowly and leave a little in the pitcher to taste later.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted over the summer and sold from autumn with the harvest year stated; many sellers deliberately hold lao cong back a year or two because the heavy roast and the woody depth integrate with rest. It keeps well for five years or more sealed and dry, and genuinely old lots are sold as aged yancha with the year on the label.
description:
Lao cong Shui Xian is Shui Xian made from old bushes, and it is the Wuyi tea for people who care more about texture and aftertaste than about perfume. The claim on the label is about plant age: cong means bush, and lao cong is usually taken to mean plants of fifty or sixty years and up, with gao cong (tall bush) used for the thirty-to-fifty-year middle ground. There is no legal definition, so the term is only as honest as the seller.

The cultivar is the same Shui Xian that fills the mountain, but a Shui Xian bush left to grow for decades becomes a small tree with thick, lichen-covered trunks and large, leathery leaves. Those leaves carry more stem and vein material and a different chemistry, and after a medium or heavy charcoal roast they give the flavour the trade calls cong wei: moss, bark, wet stone, a resinous coolness, sitting under the normal honey and orchid of the cultivar.

It is not a loud tea. The first steep is roast and dark honey; by the third the body is thick and oily; from the fifth onward the woody, mineral finish is the whole point, and it keeps going long after the liquor turns pale. Brew hot and with a full gaiwan or pot, and do not rush to judge it on the first cup: lao cong is a mid-session tea, and the aftertaste is where the money went.

Most genuine old bushes stand in the core scenic area (Hui Yuan Keng and the gorges around it are the classic sources) and in old gardens of Jianyang and Jianou outside Wuyi, which produce honest lao cong at lower prices. Look for very long, intact strips, a roast that smells sweet rather than scorched, and a seller who states the harvest and roast year. Be wary of cheap tea labelled lao cong with thin, short leaf: age cannot be faked in the cup, but it is faked on labels constantly.

If you want to learn what the old-bush note actually is, taste an ordinary Shui Xian and a lao cong from the same maker in the same sitting; the difference is obvious from the second steep.
sources_note: Age thresholds for lao cong versus gao cong vary between vendors (30, 50 or 60 years are all quoted); there is no regulated definition.
history:
Lao Cong Shui Xian is less a separate tea than a claim about the age of the plant: Shui Xian from old bushes, some said to reach 200 years. Chen De Hua sets the line at 50 years or more, but no rule fixes it, and the figure quoted varies by seller.

What the name promises is cong wei, the old-bush aroma, a woody note credited to the trunk and branches and to the surroundings the bush has grown in. That note is what sets it apart from ordinary Shui Xian.
